title: Build vs. buy for agentic AI in a regulated stack
linkedinPost:
40% of enterprise AI agent projects will be cancelled before 2027. (Gartner, June 2025)

Most of those cancellations won't be because the model failed. They'll be because the procurement decision couldn't survive regulatory scrutiny.

In regulated financial services, the build vs. buy question for agentic AI has four answers — not two. And most procurement conversations start from the wrong axis.

The 5 questions I'd answer before signing any AI vendor contract:

• Is this use case high-risk under EU AI Act Annex III? If yes, build — Article 12 logging must live in your infrastructure, not your vendor's
• Does the workflow touch customer PII or transaction data? If yes, verify EU-sovereign inference before signing anything
• Is this a competitive differentiator or a commodity function? Commodity → buy. Differentiator → build
• Do you have orchestration capacity internally? If not, buy while you build it — Claude API + n8n lower the bar more than most teams realise
• What's the 12-month volume? Low volume = buy. High volume = build economics change earlier than expected

Klarna built a custom agentic layer on top of OpenAI — not a pure buy, not from scratch. $60M saved, 853 FTE-equivalents, 82% faster resolution. Then over-automated and had to reverse course. The architecture worked. The governance design didn't follow it.

Revenue per employee rises when AI is matched to the right decision framework — not when procurement wins on year-one unit economics.

Full piece + the Regulated Stack Decision Grid I use with every client — link in comments.

mainEntity.name: What does the EU AI Act say about buying AI agents from vendors?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under EU AI Act Article 25, purchasing and deploying a third-party AI system makes you the deployer with defined obligations — even if you did not build the system. For high-risk use cases (Annex III), you are responsible for human oversight documentation, post-market monitoring, and user transparency requirements. The vendor is the provider. Core obligations for new systems apply from August 2, 2026.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to build a production-grade AI agent for a regulated firm?

acceptedAnswer.text: Using modern orchestration tooling — Claude API, n8n, Supabase — a production-grade agent for a focused use case can be scoped and shipped in 4–8 weeks by one experienced AI operator. Building regulatory-grade agentic capability across all five components from scratch takes 18–36 months. The primary variable is infrastructure decision-making at the start of the build, not model development.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my agentic AI use case is high-risk under the EU AI Act?

acceptedAnswer.text: Review EU AI Act Annex III. Financial services high-risk categories include credit scoring, insurance risk pricing, biometric identity assessment, and employment vetting. If your agent contributes to any of these decisions — including as a summarisation, first-draft, or recommendation layer — you are likely in scope for high-risk obligations. Core requirements apply from August 2, 2026 for new systems.

mainEntity.name: Should financial services firms build or buy AI agents for compliance workflows?

acceptedAnswer.text: Build — or at minimum, build the logging and memory layer even if you buy the inference. Compliance workflows in regulated financial services require full audit trail control under EU AI Act Article 12, verifiable data residency under GDPR Article 44, and customisable decision logic that most horizontal vendor solutions cannot reliably provide. The U.S. CLOUD Act creates a data jurisdiction conflict for EU firms using US-controlled cloud inference, even with EU data residency contracts in place.
